title: Flutter interview questions
tagline: The three trees, lifecycle, keys, async, and how Flutter compares with React Native.
intro: Flutter interviews circle back to one idea: UI = f(state). Most questions are that idea seen from a different side.

blocks.caption: What happens to each tree when setState runs.

items.label: Widget tree
items.detail: Immutable blueprints from build(), thrown away and recreated on every rebuild
explain: A widget is a plain Dart object describing configuration: Text('Hi') is a few fields, which is why creating thousands per frame is cheap.
It holds no state and does no layout. Its React counterpart is the JSX element in the virtual DOM.

items.label: Element tree
items.detail: Long-lived instances that diff new widgets against old and keep State alive
explain: When build() returns a widget of the same type and key at the same spot, the element keeps itself and just takes the new configuration.
The State object of a StatefulWidget lives here, which is why a counter survives a rebuild. BuildContext is a handle to this element.
It plays the role of React's reconciler and Fiber nodes: the layer that decides what actually changed.

items.label: Render tree
items.detail: RenderObjects that measure, position and paint; expensive, so reused wherever possible
explain: RenderBox, RenderFlex and RenderParagraph do layout and painting. They update only when layout or paint data really changed.
Flutter paints them itself through Skia or Impeller, rather than asking the platform for native views. The React analogue is the real DOM.

rows: What is Flutter, and why Dart?
Google's UI SDK for mobile, web and desktop from one codebase, released in 2017. Dart compiles AOT to native ARM for speed and JIT in development for hot reload.
A handle to a widget's place in the tree. It finds ancestors, e.g. Theme.of(context) or Navigator.of(context), and is how InheritedWidget data flows down.
Stateless has only final fields and a build(). Stateful has a separate State object that setState rebuilds, with initState and dispose around it.
Hot reload injects code into the running VM and keeps state, in under a second. Hot restart reruns main() and clears state; needed after changing main or initState.
The project's config: dependencies and plugins, the assets to bundle such as images and fonts, and metadata such as name and version.
A Future delivers one value then completes, e.g. GET /user/1, drawn with FutureBuilder. A Stream delivers many over time, e.g. a WebSocket, drawn with StreamBuilder.

sections.title: StatefulWidget lifecycle
sections.summary: In the order Flutter calls them.

items: createState() creates the State object that will live in the element.
initState() runs once: set up controllers, listeners and the first fetch. setState is not allowed yet.
didChangeDependencies() runs right after, and again when an InheritedWidget it reads changes.
build() runs after each of the above and every setState, and returns the widget tree.
didUpdateWidget(oldWidget) runs when the parent rebuilds with new configuration; compare widget with oldWidget.
dispose() runs when the State leaves for good: cancel timers, dispose controllers, close streams.

body: A TextEditingController or AnimationController not disposed in dispose() is a memory leak, and the most common one in Flutter code reviews.
